t.1.224.2: Tormented on account of his sons, he said this to Lapitā: "How, O Lapitā, will my little sons fare, unable as they are to fly?"
t.1.224.1: Mandapāla too, O Kauravya, brooding then over his sons, was by no means untormented, even though he had already spoken to the hot-rayed one.
t.1.224.3: As the fire grows and the wind blows swiftly, my sons will be unable to escape.
t.1.224.4: How, then, will their poor mother fare, unable to protect them, overcome with sorrow as she sees no way to save her sons?
t.1.224.6: How is my son Jaritāri, and how is my Sārisṛkka? How is Stambamitra, how is Droṇa, and how is that poor woman?
t.1.224.7: As the seer Mandapāla lamented thus again and again in the forest, Lapitā answered him with these words, as if in jealousy, O Bhārata.
t.1.224.5: How indeed, tormented, crying out and running about on every side, shall I save my sons, who are unable to crawl or to fly?
t.1.224.8: You have no concern for your sons; of those seers you have said, “They are full of splendor and mighty; they have no fear of the blazing fire.”
t.1.224.9: For in my presence you likewise entrusted them to Agni for protection, and the great-souled Fire-god promised, “So be it.”
t.1.224.10: The guardian of the world will never in any way speak an untrue word, and they are capable and able to speak for themselves; your mind is not on them.
t.1.224.11: But you torment yourself thinking only of her, my rival; surely you have no love for me such as you once had for her.
t.1.224.12: For it is in no way proper for one who has wings and the strength to act to look on without affection while his own self, in the persons of his dear ones, is being tormented.
t.1.224.13: Go then to Jaritā herself, for whose sake you are so tormented; I too shall wander alone, as one does who is tied to a worthless man.
t.1.224.15: The dull-witted man who abandons what is present and clings to a matter yet to come is despised by the world; do as you wish.
t.1.224.14: I do not roam the world in the way you imagine; I wander for the sake of my offspring, and that offspring of mine has fallen into peril.
t.1.224.16: For this blazing fire, licking at the trees, produces in my heart a hateful, inauspicious torment.
t.1.224.17: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When the fire had passed beyond that place, Jaritā, longing for her sons, hastened straight to her little children.
t.1.224.18: Wailing loudly and wretched, she saw in the forest all her sons safe and sound, released from Jātavedas.
t.1.224.20: Then Mandapāla too came there in haste, O Bhārata; but all his sons, every one of them, did not welcome him.
t.1.224.19: Again and again she gained the sight of them, a sight most beyond belief, and, crying aloud, she went to those sons one by one.
t.1.224.22: Which one is your eldest son, and which one comes next after him? Which is your middle son, and which one is your youngest?
t.1.224.21: Though the ṛṣi kept speaking again and again to each one of them and to Jaritā, they said not a single word to him, whether good or bad.
t.1.224.23: Why do you not answer me as I speak thus, afflicted with sorrow? I did what I could with the Eater of Oblations, yet I find no peace from it at all.
t.1.224.24: What concern of yours is the eldest son, or the one born after him? And what concern of yours is the middle one, or the youngest, that poor ascetic?
t.1.224.25: You who long ago abandoned me, utterly forsaken, and went away, go then to that same Lapitā, the young woman with the lovely smile!
t.1.224.27: For even Arundhatī, the virtuous and auspicious lady renowned throughout all the worlds, harbored suspicion against Vasiṣṭha, the best of seers.
t.1.224.26: For women there is nothing else in the world apart from another man, except rivalry with a co-wife; for that is how it is bound to be.
t.1.224.28: And she scorned that heroic sage, utterly pure in nature, ever devoted to what was dear and beneficial, who stands in the midst of the Seven Seers.
t.1.224.29: Because of that ill-will, she now shines with a dim radiance like reddish smoke; scarcely visible, now seen and now unseen, and unlovely, she appears like an ill omen.
t.1.224.31: A man should never in any way place his trust in a woman merely because she is his wife, for a wife who has sons no longer gives thought to her duty toward him.
t.1.224.30: Likewise you too, now that things have come to this, have abandoned me, your beloved, who came here for the sake of offspring, and you behave in just the same way.
t.1.224.32: Then all those sons duly attended upon him, and he, O king, began to comfort his own offspring.
